summary: This unit teaches you to prepare a written quotation for a job in your trade, such as a steel gate or new electrical outlets. You will learn to find out what the customer needs, measure on site, work out quantities, materials, labour and other costs, and add markup and GCT to reach a fair price. You will also learn what a quotation must show, how to check it, present it and follow it up, and how to handle acceptance and changes to the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423), and electrical installation trainees take the same unit. It teaches you to **prepare a quotation**: a written offer to do stated work for a stated price. You will measure a job, work out what it will cost the business, add a fair profit, and set the price and terms out clearly for the customer.

Pricing is where many small trade businesses go wrong. Price too low and you work for nothing, or cut corners; price too high and the customer goes elsewhere; leave the terms unclear and you end up arguing over the bill. A clear, checked quotation protects both the business and the customer.

**Who it is for:** trainees in welding and fabrication, electrical installation and other trades. You need simple arithmetic: adding, multiplying, percentages, and changing millimetres to metres. A calculator or a spreadsheet helps, but you must be able to check the sums yourself.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Find out what the customer needs
Ask the right questions about the work, the timing and the budget, and visit the site to measure and look for problems.
Make a take-off list from a drawing or sketch, change it into stock lengths or rolls, and add an allowance for waste.
Get current supplier prices, compare suppliers, and include consumables and fixings.
Cost the labour and other costs
Estimate the hours, work out the labour cost, and add transport, hire and other job costs.
Add a markup for overheads and profit, and GCT at the current rate where the business is registered.
Set out the description, prices and terms clearly on the business's form.
Check every figure, get approval, explain the quotation to the customer, and follow it up.
Get a signed acceptance, and price any change to the work in writing as a variation.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on quotations and estimates, customer requirements, site visits and measuring, quantities, material and labour costs, other costs, markup and profit, GCT, the contents and terms of a quotation, checking, presenting, acceptance, changes and records. Several questions are short calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and figures, such as GCT, take-off, variation, tender, a deposit or a profit worked out in J$) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** in a group: measuring a job at the Centre and preparing a costing sheet; then writing a full quotation, presenting it to a "customer" and pricing an extra item as a variation.

blocks.note: Show your working on every calculation and check it a second way. Most marks lost on pricing questions come from a missed item or a slip in the sums, not from not knowing the method.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **quotation** (quote) is a written offer to do **stated work** for a **stated price**, usually for a set time. Once the customer accepts it, the business is expected to do that work for that price.

head: Document
What it is
When
rows: An approximate price, the business's best guess; the final price may be different
When the work cannot yet be fully known, or the customer wants a rough idea
A firm price for clearly described work, valid for a stated time
Before the work, once the job has been measured and costed
A formal offer to do a large job, sent in by a closing date against other businesses
When a client, often a public body or large company, invites tenders
An agreed change to the work, and its price, after the quotation has been accepted
The bill asking the customer to pay
When the work, or a stage of it, is done
Proof that the customer has paid

blocks.p: When the customer signs to accept a quotation, the business and the customer have made an agreement, a **contract**. The quotation becomes the record of what was agreed: the work, the price and the terms. That is why it must be clear and correct.

flow: Talk to the customer: what they want, when, and any budget
Visit the site to measure and look for anything that affects the work
Make a sketch with all the sizes
Take off the materials and quantities; add a waste allowance
Get current prices; cost the materials, consumables and fixings
Estimate the labour; add transport, hire and other costs
Add the markup, then GCT at the current rate where it applies
Write the quotation with the description, prices and terms
Check every figure; get the supervisor's approval
Send or present it; keep a copy; follow it up

sections.title: The customer's needs and the site visit

blocks.h: Finding out what the customer wants

blocks.p: Before you can price a job, you must know **exactly what work the customer wants done**. Ask, listen and write it down.

head: Ask about
Examples
rows: What is to be made, fitted or installed; how many; sizes; design; finish or colour
Tube size or bar size; galvanised or painted; type of fittings
When it is needed; any dates when the site cannot be used
Whether the customer has a figure in mind, so you can suggest options
Address, access, parking, power supply, who will be there

blocks.note: How much the customer earns, or what the last customer paid, is not part of the job and has no place in the price. Price the work, not the person.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **site visit** lets you measure and see problems that affect the work and the price before you commit to a figure.

ul: Arrive on time, introduce yourself and ask the customer to show you exactly what they want.
Measure each opening, wall or run carefully with a **tape measure**, at least twice, and write the sizes on a neat sketch. Number each window, door or position.
Check the condition of walls, frames and floors: weak blocks or rotten frames change the fixings and the work.
Electrical work: note where the supply and the distribution board are, the cable routes and the wall type, and whether the existing wiring looks old or damaged. Look only: never open live equipment.
Check access: parking, stairs, height, and whether a ladder, scaffold tower or generator is needed.
Note safety issues: children, dogs, a busy road, overhead lines.
Take photos, with the customer's permission, and confirm the main details with the customer before you leave.

blocks.note: Measure from the floor or a stable step. Never stand on chairs, drums or tables to measure, and do not open sockets, switches or the distribution board. Keep the tape under control: a steel tape that snaps back can cut you.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Perimeter** (the distance round the edge) of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width). A frame 2.0 m × 1.2 m needs 2 × (2.0 + 1.2) = 6.4 m round the outside.
**Area** of a rectangle = length × width, in square metres (m²). An opening 1.5 m × 2.1 m has an area of 3.15 m².
Change millimetres to metres **before** you work out an area in m²: 900 mm × 2100 mm = 0.9 m × 2.1 m = 1.89 m².

blocks.note: Jamaica uses metric units, but many steel sections and fittings are still sold by inch sizes or in 20-foot lengths (about 6.1 m). Check how your supplier describes and sells each item, and work in millimetres and metres on your sketch.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **take-off** is a list of every material and item, with its size and quantity, worked out from the drawing or your site sketch. Go through the drawing part by part, so nothing is missed.

A steel gate 1.0 m wide and 1.6 m high: a frame of 25 mm square tube with a middle rail, eight infill bars of 12 mm square bar, two weld-on hinges and a latch. The supplier sells tube and bar in 6 m lengths.

head: Item
Working
Total needed
Plus 10% waste
Buy
rows: Electrodes, cutting and grinding discs, wire brush

ul: **Round up to whole stock lengths or rolls.** You cannot buy 2.35 lengths: 14.08 m ÷ 6 m = 2.35, so you buy 3.
Check with a **cutting list**: each 6 m bar gives three pieces of 1.6 m (4.8 m), so eight pieces need three bars. The cutting list and the rounding should agree.
Add a **waste allowance** for offcuts, saw cuts and mistakes. 10% is a common figure; your workplace may use another.
Do not forget **consumables** (used up on the job: electrodes, discs, gas, primer, paint) and **fixings** (bolts, screws, wall plugs, anchors, saddles, cable ties).

head: Item
Working
Buy
rows: PVC conduit, sold in 3 m lengths
Couplers, bends, saddles, boxes, screws and wall plugs, from the sketch
As counted, plus a few spare

ul: Use **current** supplier price lists or written quotes from suppliers. Old price lists, a friend's price or a guess are not good enough: prices change.
Read the **price unit**: per metre, per length, per roll, each, per box or per litre. J$480 per metre is not J$480 per length.
Compare suppliers on **total cost** (including delivery), **quality**, **delivery time** and whether they have the **stock**.

head: Comparing two suppliers for 4 lengths of tube
Supplier A
Supplier B

flow: Break the job into tasks: cutting, fitting, welding, grinding, painting, fitting on site; or chasing walls, running conduit and cable, fixing boxes, connecting, testing
Estimate the hours for each task, using records of similar jobs and the advice of experienced workers
Add time for travel, setting up and cleaning up
Work out the **worker-hours**: number of workers × hours each
Labour cost = worker-hours × the labour rate

blocks.p: At a labour rate of J$1,000 per worker-hour, labour = 16 × J$1,000 = **J$16,000**.

ul: A team job: 2 workers for 4 days of 8 hours = 2 × 4 × 8 = 64 worker-hours.
Never pick a number of hours just to make the price look low. Under-estimated labour is the commonest reason small jobs lose money.

head: Cost
Examples
rows: Fuel or van hire to take workers and materials to the site and back, perhaps several trips; often forgotten on jobs away from the workshop
A scaffold tower, generator or lifting equipment the business does not own
Harnesses for work at height; a permit the client requires
A crane, a mason for the gateposts, a plumber

blocks.p: **Overheads** are the running costs of the business that no single job causes: rent, electricity, water, insurance, phone and internet, office costs, and the wear and replacement of tools and machines. They must be covered by every job, either built into the labour rate or added in the markup. A business that forgets its overheads can be busy every day and still lose money.

head: Direct job costs
Overheads
rows: Materials, consumables and fixings for this job
Hire of equipment for this job

blocks.h: Adding up the costs for the gate

blocks.p: A **markup** is an amount added to the costs, usually a percentage of them, to cover overheads and give a **profit**. Profit lets the business replace tools and machines, cover slow months and customers who do not pay, pay its owner, and grow.
Profit = price − costs. A job costing J$42,000 that sells for J$50,000 makes a profit of J$8,000.

blocks.note: **Markup** is worked on the cost; **margin** is the profit as a share of the selling price. A 25% markup on J$46,200 gives J$11,550 profit, which is only 20% of the J$57,750 price. Do not mix the two up.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Price too low
Price much too high
rows: The business may not cover its costs and loses money on the job
It may be tempted to cut corners, leading to poor or unsafe work
It has nothing to fall back on if something goes wrong
The customer goes to another business and the work is lost
The business gets a name for being overpriced

blocks.p: A **fair price** covers all the costs and a reasonable profit, and matches the quality and service offered.

head: Sum
Working
Answer
rows: 10% waste allowance on J$36,000 of materials

blocks.p: A discount comes straight out of the profit. On the gate, a 10% discount (J$5,775) takes the price to J$51,975 and **halves** the profit, from J$11,550 to J$5,775. Only the person with the authority, usually the owner or supervisor, agrees discounts. If a customer asks for one, explain what the price includes and pass the request on.

ul: **GCT** stands for **General Consumption Tax**, Jamaica's tax on most goods and services, collected by Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ).

A business that is **registered** for GCT must charge it at the **current rate** and show it on its quotations and bills. Small businesses below the registration level may not be registered; your employer will tell you.
On a quotation, show GCT as a **separate line** after the subtotal, at the current rate: never hidden in the labour or added as a surprise on the bill.
In class and in the practical, use the rate the assessor gives you, and check it is the current one when you work.

blocks.p: A quotation should be **neat, clear and on the business's letterhead or quotation form**, typed or written in ink, never sent only as a voice note.

head: Part
What it shows
rows: Name, address, phone, email, and any tax numbers (TRN; GCT registration number if registered)
Its own number and the date, so it can be found and matched to the job later
Name, address and phone; the job address if different

Exactly what will be done, with sizes, materials and finish: "Make and fit one pedestrian gate, 1.0 m × 1.6 m, 25 mm square tube frame, 12 mm square bar infill, two weld-on hinges and latch, primed and painted black"
Item by item or in sections (materials, labour, other costs), then the subtotal, GCT at the current rate if it applies, and the total
How long the price stands, for example 30 days
How much is paid when, and how: for example 50% deposit on acceptance, balance on completion, by cash or bank transfer
What is **not** included, so the customer knows what to arrange: masonry for the gateposts, making good walls or painting after electrical work
What is guaranteed and for how long, for example workmanship for 12 months
Name and signature of the person issuing it, and a space for the customer to sign and date their acceptance

head: Line
Detail
rows: Hillside Steel Works (a made-up business), Mandeville, Manchester. Tel. 876-000-0000
Mrs P. Edwards, 14 Orchid Close (made-up details)

Make and fit one pedestrian gate, 1.0 m × 1.6 m: 25 mm square tube frame with middle rail, eight 12 mm square bar infills, two weld-on hinges and a latch; primed and painted black; fitted to the existing pillars
50% deposit on acceptance; balance on completion, cash or bank transfer
Start within 5 working days of the deposit; finish within 7 working days
Excludes building or repairing the pillars
Issued by: ________  Accepted by customer: ________  Date: ________

blocks.p: Here the markup has been built into each line: materials at J$25,200 × 1.25 = J$31,500, labour J$16,000 × 1.25 = J$20,000, transport J$5,000 × 1.25 = J$6,250. Most businesses show customers the selling price of each part, not their own costs; your workplace decides how much detail to show.

head: Term
Why it is there
rows: Material prices change; after the date the business may check the price again
Helps buy the materials and shows the customer is serious
The customer knows when and how to pay; no surprises
The customer knows what is not in the price and must be arranged separately
Gives the customer confidence and sets out what is covered

blocks.note: "Labour: 3 days" tells the customer nothing about what they are paying for. Describe the work, so both sides know what was agreed.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: The description matches what the customer asked for and what you measured
The take-off is checked against the drawing or sketch: no missed items, fixings, consumables or transport
Each quantity and each price is checked, and the prices are current
Every sum is worked again, or by a second person: each line, the markup, the subtotal, GCT and the total
The terms are complete: validity, deposit, payment, dates, exclusions, warranty
Customer's name, address and phone, the quotation number, the date and the spelling are right
The supervisor checks, approves and signs it
It is sent, and a copy is filed

blocks.note: A junior worker who has priced a job always has it checked and approved before it is sent. Never send it early to please the customer, or lower the price or leave out labour to make it look cheaper.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Give it in the way the customer prefers (in person, by email or message) and offer to go through it.
Explain the work included, the materials, the price and the terms in plain words, and point out what is **not** included.
Listen to questions and answer honestly. Never tell a customer they must decide today.
If the customer says the price is higher than another business's, explain what yours includes: the materials, the warranty, safe work, the finish. Do not run the other business down.
Offer a cheaper option where there is one, such as a simpler design, but never cut corners on safety.
Refer discounts and anything outside your authority to your supervisor.
Tell the customer how long the price is valid and how to accept it.
Record the date each quotation was sent.
If you hear nothing after about a week, contact the customer politely to ask whether they have any questions.
Keep a copy of every quotation, so the price can be checked when the job is done and billed, and so disputes can be settled.
A simple quotation register helps: number, date, customer, job, amount, status (sent, accepted, lost) and follow-up date.
Keep the business's costings and price lists private, so competitors cannot use them to undercut you.

sections.title: Acceptance and changes to the job

ul: The customer accepts by **signing and dating** the acceptance part of the quotation (or sending written acceptance). That makes the agreement, the contract, clear.
Collect the deposit, as the terms say, and give a receipt.
Check that the acceptance is within the validity period. If it is late, check current prices and confirm the price or send a revised quotation.
Order materials and book the work.

blocks.p: A **variation** is an agreed change to the work, and its price, after the quotation has been accepted. It happens when the customer asks for extra or different work, or when a problem is found that nobody knew about when the price was agreed.

flow: Do not just do the extra work and add it to the bill, and do not ignore a problem
Explain to the customer that it is not in the quotation
If a problem makes part of the work unsafe, stop that part and show the customer
Work out the extra materials, labour, time and other costs, and add the markup, as for any job
Give the customer a written price for the change: the variation
Tell your supervisor
Go ahead only when the customer has agreed the change and its price in writing
File the variation with the job papers, so the final bill matches what was agreed

head: Variation example: a matching letterbox for the gate
Amount
rows: J$5,500 (plus GCT at the current rate if registered)

blocks.p: The invoice for the balance = the quotation total + agreed variations − the deposit already paid. Example (a business not registered for GCT): a J$300,000 job with a 40% deposit (J$120,000) and a J$25,000 variation: 300,000 + 25,000 − 120,000 = **J$205,000** to pay.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work through its examples again.

ul: I can explain the difference between an estimate, a quotation, a tender, a variation, an invoice and a receipt.
I can find out what a customer needs and carry out a safe site visit, measuring twice and sketching.
I can change between millimetres and metres and work out lengths, perimeters and areas.
I can make a take-off list, round up to stock lengths or rolls, and add a waste allowance.
I can get current prices, read price units, and compare suppliers.
I can estimate labour in worker-hours and work out the labour cost.
I can list other job costs, and explain what overheads are and how they are covered.
I can add a markup, work out profit, and explain the difference between markup and margin.
I can work out a discount and a deposit, and show GCT correctly at the current rate.
I can write a quotation with all the details and terms it needs, and explain why each term is there.
I can check a quotation, get it approved, present it and follow it up.
I can handle acceptance, and price and record a variation.

terms: Materials used up on a job, such as electrodes, discs and gas
The agreement made when the customer accepts the quotation
Part of the price paid in advance, to buy materials and confirm the order
An amount taken off the price; it comes out of the profit
An approximate price that may change
Work or items that are not included in the price
General Consumption Tax, charged at the current rate by registered businesses
The bill asking the customer to pay
The amount charged or costed for one worker for one hour
Profit as a share of the selling price
An amount added to the costs to cover overheads and give a profit
The business's running costs, such as rent and electricity, that no single job causes
When and how the customer must pay
The distance round the edge of a shape
The selling price minus all the costs
A written offer to do stated work for a stated price
Proof that the customer has paid
A computer program with rows and columns, often used for costings
A business that sells materials to your business
A list of all the materials and quantities worked out from a drawing
A formal offer for a large job, sent in by a closing date against other businesses
How long the price on a quotation stands
An agreed change to the work, and its price, after acceptance
The business's promise about what is guaranteed, and for how long
Number of workers × hours each worked

c1.title: A carport frame in Bog Walk
c1.text: Kevin, a welding trainee, goes with his supervisor to price a steel carport at a house in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The carport roof is to be 5.4 m long and 3.0 m wide, on six posts of 75 mm square tube, which the supplier sells in 6 m lengths. On site, Kevin finds that the driveway slopes: four posts must be 2.4 m long, but the two back posts must be 2.55 m. Two suppliers quote for the 75 mm tube: Supplier A, J$9,800 per length with free delivery; Supplier B, J$9,200 per length plus J$2,500 for delivery.

c2.title: A pharmacy's sliding gate in St Ann's Bay
c2.text: Nadine is a junior estimator at a fabrication business in St Ann's Bay, St Ann. She is pricing a sliding security gate for a pharmacy. Her costing sheet shows: materials J$84,000; labour for 3 workers for 3 days of 8 hours, at J$1,100 per worker-hour; transport J$6,000; and hire of a generator for the site J$7,500. The business adds a 25% markup to its total costs, and only the owner may agree discounts.

c3.title: A kitchen circuit in Hayes
c3.text: Shaquille, an electrical installation trainee, helps his supervisor price a new kitchen circuit with three double socket outlets for a house in Hayes, Clarendon. His take-off shows 13 m of PVC conduit, which the supplier sells in 3 m lengths, as well as the cable, boxes and sockets. The quotation, dated 1 September, says "Price valid for 30 days". The customer phones on 20 October to accept it.

c4.title: A gazebo frame in Discovery Bay
c4.text: A small fabrication business in Discovery Bay, St Ann, which is not registered for GCT, is building a steel gazebo frame at a villa. The customer signed a quotation for J$420,000, with a 50% deposit on acceptance and the balance on completion. Halfway through the job she asks for a matching steel bench. Then, while digging for one of the posts, the team finds a buried water pipe exactly where the post should go.

c5.title: A draft quotation in Black River
c5.text: A new worker at a fabrication business in Black River, St Elizabeth, has drafted a quotation for four steel security doors for a school about 40 km away. It shows: Materials J$96,500; Labour J$48,000; Transport J$0; Subtotal J$154,500. There is no quotation number, no date, the payment terms say "TBA", and nothing says how long the price is valid. The supervisor has not yet seen it.

questions.q: Allowing for the slope, how many 6 m lengths of 75 mm tube must Kevin price for the six posts?
questions.why: Four posts at 2.4 m and two at 2.55 m make 14.7 m. Each 6 m length gives two posts, so six posts need 3 lengths; 14.7 ÷ 6 = 2.45 also rounds up to 3. You cannot buy part of a length.

questions.q: What is the area of the carport roof?
questions.why: Area is length × width: 5.4 × 3.0 = 16.2 m². 16.8 m is the perimeter (the distance round the edge), which you would need for edge trim, not for roof sheets.

questions.q: What should Kevin do about the sloping driveway?
o: Note it on his sketch and price the longer back posts
Leave it out, since the customer did not mention it
Tell the customer to level the driveway first, free
Price all six posts the same and cut them on the day
questions.why: A site visit is for finding exactly what affects the work and the price. Recording the slope on the sketch means the right lengths are ordered and priced, with no surprises later.

questions.q: For the 3 lengths of tube, which supplier is cheaper, and by how much?
questions.why: A: 3 × 9,800 = J$29,400. B: 3 × 9,200 = J$27,600, plus J$2,500 delivery = J$30,100. Compare the full cost, delivery included, and then quality, delivery time and stock.

questions.q: What is the labour cost for the gate?
questions.why: Worker-hours = 3 workers × 3 days × 8 hours = 72, and 72 × J$1,100 = J$79,200. Leaving out a day or a worker is a common way to under-price a job.

questions.q: What price, before GCT, should go on the quotation?
questions.why: Total costs are 84,000 + 79,200 + 6,000 + 7,500 = J$176,700. The 25% markup adds J$44,175, giving J$220,875. The markup goes on all the costs, not only the materials.

questions.q: The pharmacy owner asks Nadine for 10% off. What should she do?
o: Say she will ask the owner, who decides on discounts
Agree at once, so that the pharmacy does not go elsewhere
Refuse, and say the price can never be changed
Take 10% off the labour only, as she worked it out
questions.why: A discount comes straight out of the profit, so only someone with the authority, here the owner, agrees it. Nadine can explain what the price includes and pass the request on promptly.

questions.q: How many 3 m lengths of conduit must be priced?
questions.why: 13 ÷ 3 = 4.33, and you cannot buy a third of a length, so round up to 5. With a 10% waste allowance (14.3 m) the answer is still 5.

questions.q: Which items are the most easily forgotten in Shaquille's take-off?
o: The three double socket outlets and their boxes
Conduit couplers, saddles, screws and wall plugs
The cable for the new kitchen circuit
The 13 m of PVC conduit itself
questions.why: The main items are on the drawing, but fittings and fixings are not. Couplers, bends, saddles, screws, wall plugs and cable ties add up; a good take-off lists every item.

questions.q: What should happen when the customer accepts on 20 October?
o: Start work at the old price, since the customer has accepted
Check current prices, then confirm or revise the quotation
Refuse the job, because the quotation has run out
Add 30% to the price to cover the late reply
questions.why: The price was valid only until about 1 October. After that, prices for cable and fittings may have changed, so the business checks them and either confirms the price in writing or sends a revised quotation.

questions.q: How should the business work out the price for the bench?
o: Charge 10% of the original quotation, as a rule of thumb
Ask the customer what she thinks would be fair to pay for it
Add it free of charge, since she has already paid a deposit
Cost its materials, labour and other costs, and add markup
questions.why: Extra work is priced the same way as the main job, then given to the customer in writing as a variation. Guessing or giving it away loses money and leads to arguments.

questions.q: Who should decide what to do about the water pipe?
o: The customer, once the options and costs are explained
The team, who should move the pipe themselves to save time
The team, who should move the post without telling anyone
Nobody: the team should fill the hole and carry on as planned
questions.why: The pipe was not known when the price was agreed. The business stops that part, shows the customer, explains the choices (move the post, or have a plumber move the pipe) with their costs, and goes ahead only on her written agreement.

questions.q: The customer agrees the bench as a variation of J$38,500. What is the balance to pay on completion?
What is wrong with the subtotal on the draft?
questions.why: 96,500 + 48,000 = 144,500, so the draft is J$10,000 too high. Every sum on a quotation is worked out a second time, or by a second person, before it goes out.

questions.q: Which cost has been left out that will lose the business money?
o: The labour for making and fitting the doors
Transport to and from the school, 40 km away
The steel and fittings for the four doors
Printing the quotation on the letterhead
questions.why: Transport is shown as J$0, but the team and the doors must travel 40 km each way, perhaps more than once. Travel is one of the costs most often forgotten on jobs away from the workshop.

questions.q: Before the quotation is sent, what else must be done?
o: Send it now and put the missing details on the final bill
Lower the total so the school accepts it more quickly
Add the number, date and terms, then get it approved
Print it in colour so that it looks more official
questions.why: A quotation needs its own number and date, clear terms and a check of every figure. The supervisor approves it before it goes out, and a copy is filed.

questions.q: A shop sells a grill for J$100,000. Making and fitting it cost the shop J$80,000. What percentage of the selling price is profit?
questions.why: The profit is 100,000 − 80,000 = J$20,000, and J$20,000 is 20% of J$100,000. Notice that J$20,000 is a 25% markup on the cost: markup is worked on the cost, margin on the selling price.

questions.q: When a job is finished, which document asks the customer to pay the balance?
questions.why: The quotation offers the price before the work; the invoice (the bill) asks for payment after it; the receipt proves that payment was made.

questions.q: A price list gives 12 mm square bar at J$480 per metre. What do three 6 m lengths cost?
questions.why: Three lengths of 6 m are 18 m, and 18 × J$480 = J$8,640. Always check the price unit: per metre, per length or each.

questions.q: Which of these is an overhead rather than a cost of one particular job?
o: The electrodes used up on this job
Hire of a scaffold tower for this job
Fuel to drive to this customer's site
questions.why: Overheads are the business's running costs, such as rent, electricity and insurance, that no single job causes. They are covered in the labour rate or the markup; the other three are direct costs of the job.
